{{Short description|Type of stochastic Markov process}}
In the mathematical study of [[stochastic process]]es, a '''Harris chain''' is a [[Markov chain]] where the chain returns to a particular part of the state space an unbounded number of times.<ref>{{Cite book | first1 = Søren | last1 = Asmussen| doi = 10.1007/0-387-21525-5_7 | chapter = Further Topics in Renewal Theory and Regenerative Processes | title = Applied Probability and Queues | series = Stochastic Modelling and Applied Probability | volume = 51 | pages = 186–219 | year = 2003 | isbn = 978-0-387-00211-8 }}</ref> Harris chains are [[regenerative process]]es and are named after [[Ted Harris (mathematician)|Theodore Harris]]. The theory of Harris chains and Harris recurrence is useful for treating Markov chains on general (possibly uncountably infinite) state spaces.

==Definition==

Let <math>\{X_n\}</math> be a [[Markov chain]] on a general state space <math>\Omega</math> with [[stochastic kernel]] <math>K</math>. The kernel represents a generalized one-step transition probability law, so that <math>P(X_{n+1}\in C\mid X_n=x)=K(x,C)</math> for all states <math>x</math> in <math>\Omega</math> and all measurable sets <math>C\subseteq \Omega</math>.  The chain <math>\{X_n\}</math> is a ''Harris chain''<ref>R. Durrett. ''Probability: Theory and Examples''. Thomson, 2005. {{ISBN|0-534-42441-4}}.</ref> if there exists <math>A\subseteq\Omega,\varepsilon>0</math>, and [[probability measure]] <math>\rho</math> with <math>\rho(\Omega)=1</math> such that 
# If <math>\tau_A:=\inf \{n\geq 0:X_n\in A\}</math>, then <math>P(\tau_A<\infty\mid X_0=x)=1</math> for all <math>x\in\Omega</math>.
# If <math>x\in A</math> and <math>C\subseteq\Omega</math> (where <math>C</math> is measurable), then <math>K(x, C)\geq \varepsilon\rho(C)</math>.

The first part of the definition ensures that the chain returns to some state within <math>A</math> with probability 1, regardless of where it starts. It follows that it visits state <math>A</math> infinitely often (with probability 1). The second part implies that once the Markov chain is in state <math>A</math>, its next-state can be generated with the help of an independent Bernoulli coin flip. To see this, first note that the parameter <math>\varepsilon</math> must be between 0 and 1 (this can be shown by applying the second part of the definition to the set <math>C=\Omega</math>). Now let <math>x</math> be a point in <math>A</math> and suppose <math>X_n=x</math>.  To choose the next state <math>X_{n+1}</math>, independently flip a biased coin with success probability <math>\varepsilon</math>. If the coin flip is successful, choose the next state <math>X_{n+1}\in\Omega</math> according to the probability measure <math>\rho</math>. Else (and if <math>\varepsilon<1</math>), choose the next state <math>X_{n+1}</math> according to the measure <math>P(X_{n+1}\in C\mid X_n=x)=(K(x,C)-\varepsilon\rho(C))/(1-\varepsilon)</math> (defined for all measurable subsets <math>C\subseteq \Omega</math>).

Two random processes <math>\{X_n\}</math> and <math>\{Y_n\}</math> that have the same probability law and are Harris chains according to the above definition can be coupled as follows: Suppose that <math>X_n=x</math> and <math>Y_n=y</math>, where <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> are points in <math>A</math>. Using the same coin flip to decide the next-state of both processes, it follows that the next states are the same with probability at least <math>\varepsilon</math>.

==Examples==
=== Example 1: Countable state space ===

Let Ω be a countable state space. The kernel ''K'' is defined by the one-step conditional transition probabilities P[''X''<sub>''n''+1</sub> = ''y'' | ''X''<sub>''n''</sub>&nbsp;=&nbsp;''x''] for ''x'',''y'' ∈ Ω.  The measure ρ is a [[probability mass function]] on the states, so that ''ρ''(''x'')&nbsp;≥&nbsp;0 for all ''x'' ∈ Ω, and the sum of the ''ρ''(x) probabilities is equal to one.  Suppose the above definition is satisfied for 
a given set ''A'' ⊆ Ω and a given parameter ε > 0.   Then P[''X''<sub>''n''+1</sub> = ''c'' | ''X''<sub>''n''</sub> = ''x''] ≥ ''ερ''(''c'') for all ''x'' ∈ ''A'' and all ''c'' ∈ Ω.

=== Example 2: Chains with continuous densities ===

Let {''X''<sub>''n''</sub>},&nbsp;''X''<sub>''n''</sub> ∈ '''R'''<sup>''d''</sup> be a [[Markov chain]] with a [[Integral kernel|kernel]] that is [[absolutely continuous]] with respect to [[Lebesgue measure]]:

: ''K''(''x'', ''dy'') = ''K''(''x'', ''y'')&nbsp;''dy''

such that ''K''(''x'', ''y'') is a [[continuous function]].

Pick (''x''<sub>0</sub>,&nbsp;''y''<sub>0</sub>) such that ''K''(''x''<sub>0</sub>,&nbsp;''y''<sub>0</sub> )&nbsp;>&nbsp;0, and let ''A'' and Ω be [[open sets]] containing ''x''<sub>0</sub> and ''y''<sub>0</sub> respectively that are sufficiently small so that ''K''(''x'',&nbsp;''y'') ≥ ''ε'' > 0 on ''A''&nbsp;×&nbsp; Ω. Letting ''ρ''(''C'') = |Ω&nbsp;∩&nbsp;''C''|/|Ω| where |Ω| is the [[Lebesgue measure]] of Ω, we have that (2) in the above definition holds.  If (1) holds, then {''X''<sub>''n''</sub>} is a Harris chain.

==Reducibility and periodicity==

In the following <math>R:=\inf\{n\ge1:X_n\in A\}</math>; i.e. <math>R</math> is the first time after time 0 that the process enters region <math>A</math>. Let <math>\mu</math> denote the initial distribution of the Markov chain, i.e. <math>X_0\sim\mu</math>. 

'''Definition:'''   If for all <math>\mu</math>, <math>P [ R<\infty | X_0 \in A ]=1</math>, then the Harris chain is called ''recurrent.''

'''Definition:'''  A recurrent Harris chain <math>X_n</math> is ''aperiodic'' if <math>\exists N</math>, such that <math>\forall n\ge N</math>, <math>\forall \mu, P[X_n\in A | X_0 \in A]>0</math>

'''Theorem:''' Let <math>X_n</math> be an aperiodic recurrent Harris chain with stationary distribution <math>\pi</math>. If  <math>P [ R<\infty | X_0 \in A ]=1</math> then as <math>n\rightarrow\infty</math>, <math>||\mathcal{L}(X_n|X_0)-\pi||_{TV}\rightarrow 0</math> where <math>||\cdot||_{TV}</math> denotes the [[total variation]] for signed measures defined on the same [[measurable space]].
